image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Top:** Proportional symbol map / **bubble map** of U.S. counties.
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth map** of U.S. counties.

## 2. Layout techniques
- The visualization uses **two vertically stacked map panels** (small multiples by metric).
- No faceting by category within each panel.
- No stacking of marks.
- Top panel overlays **circles on a geographic basemap**; bottom panel fills **county polygons** by color.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County geographic location | Spatial/geographic | Position on map (latitude/longitude) |
| Total number of Covid cases by county in 2020 | Quantitative | Circle size/area in the top map |
| Per capita Covid cases by county in 2020 (share of population with a reported case) | Quantitative | Color/hue of county areas in the bottom map |
| County | Categorical/nominal (geographic unit) | Individual map marks/regions (one circle or one county polygon per county) |
| State names / selected place names | Categorical/nominal | Text labels on the map |
| No cases reported | Categorical/nominal | Light gray fill in the choropleth legend/map |

comments.raw_comment: Like most people have noticed, there is a lot more cases on the East side of the map compared to West side and central part of the map. I wonder why that may be? I have also come to notice that places like California and Washington, which are on the far West side I may add, are also hit pretty hard. This is most likely because of how big the population is over there and how popular of visiting places they are. Which makes sense why the more populated places have higher numbers/ more cases unlike places like Wyoming (4,100+ cases) which is more in the middle/ left side of the map which aren't as populated. Bringing up the fact that the East Coast has more than double the population than the West Coast. This also shows us that no matter how much we want to go on vacation to make up for the uneventful year we've had, we probably shouldn't if at all possible. But that brings up another question: when? When will this be over so we may not be as at risk? It's saddening to see how many people/ families this has effected and all jobs that have been lost with the amount of businesses closing/ closed down because of this.

I noticed that simply by looking at either one of the graphs, it is difficult to make an accurate inference about which region has been affected the most by the virus. By looking at the first graph, a north eastern area (including New Jersey) and the state of Florida clearly stand out in the number of cases. In contrast, by looking at the second graph, we can see that regions touching the Mississippi River definitely have had a higher number of per capita cases. The difference between the two graphs is due to the first one representing the number of cases as an absolute value, whereas the second one represents the number of cases relative to each region’s population.
I wonder how the two sets of data could be combined in order to answer the question: “Which region in the United States has been affected the most by COVID-19?” Realistically, there is no simple answer, which also means that various media sources can report varying results based on their main message. The existence of such biased information has an uncontrollable impact on the decisions made on a local level. For example, claims about the situation of the virus in New Jersey are decisive factors when evaluating the school reopening plans in the state. In this way, that information directly affects me and thousands of other students and their parents.
Finally, I believe that a catchy, yet accurate headline, that captures the graph’s main idea is “Which parts of the U.S. were hit the hardest by COVID-19?”

We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs, including “In the Red:  A Look at How Covid-19 is Affecting Different US States” by Montessori Middle School in Shreveport, Louisiana,  “What’s the State of Coronavirus?” by Natalie of San Francisco, "Keep your mask on... You can continue to post responses.  Please check back late tomorrow -- Thursday afternoon, September 17 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.  There is also a link to Covid statistics, graphs, and maps for each state and countries worldwide.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who has been quarantining since March with her extended family,  and Christine Franklin of Athens, Georgia, who has been quarantining since March with her husband, dog, and cat (and sometimes her sons).

comments.raw_comment: I notice that the maps both portray similar ideas, each with shades of red indicating their prominence in our country, and their epicenters in the same locations. They also relay the same information onto who looks upon this graph. Our eastern portion is so much more contaminated than the west, though this is due to heavy population levels and density in coastal cities. You see this in California; though not an eastern coastal city, Los Angeles has one of the biggest epicenters on the map, indicating high population. The defining line between the cases in the east and the west seems to be around the Mississippi River area. I question the east's population density, it has to be so much to display all of those cases; indicating that there might be more of an internal problem than population. I wonder what that issue could be, or what it could entail. My biggest concern has to be the spread. Covid-19 seems to have spread all across the west, where will they spread to? The mid-west looks to be low on cases, maybe there? On the other hand, in California, my community has little to no cases. I've recently tried to ignore the news, as it saddens my mood, so I'm not informed of the new cases in my town. In quarantine, we're struggling to keep the community afloat. My town is oriented around our school district and creating events for the children, but we can no longer have that privilege due to Covid-19. My catchy headline for all of this? "Covid; Where to?"

I’m noticing that both of these maps illustrate similar concepts: The Eastern US is clearly suffering more cases and contaminations than the West. Somehow, New England especially has seen great changes to their case count. So, I wonder, what do these case statistics mean for herd immunity? Are we getting closer to being able to gather again?  And why, when New England was doing so well at first, is it now on the decline in terms of public health? Are leaders becoming more lenient? Or are people just too distressed, mentally and physically, from quarantine to bother listening? Peoples’ distraught especially worries me. Fear is a powerful motivator---for good or for ill. Therefore, I’m anxious these new outbreaks will reach my community, extending online learning and endangering our hopes of having a semi-normal school year. Online learning has been tough on my mind and body, so I, and many others, are not eager to have it prolonged. At the same time, it would be nice if rising case numbers led to a greater chance of herd immunity. Of course, it’s an absolute tragedy that more people are contracting the virus, and even dying as a result, but it would be uplifting to know that they are not contaminated in vain.

comments.raw_comment: As I observed these graphs that are displaying the largest epicenters of COVID-19 in 2020, I noticed that this irking virus tends to spread in areas of high population. This can mostly be attributed to the close contact people create with one another as they walk down busy, city streets such as Michigan Avenue in Chicago and Rodeo Drive in Los Angeles. I wonder when these people that aren't taking the necessary precautions are going to realize that COVID-19 is not going away. This pandemic has caused great havoc in Glen Ellyn-a small and tight-knitted community in the western suburbs of Chicago. Students are forced to expand their learning in the confines of their homes, athletes are told that their season will be greatly minimized, and working people are laid off to accommodate their company's income-related challenges.  At the end of the day, these graphs show us where we need to reinforce rules and regulations for people at risk of COVID-19. This concludes a recap of "2020 - A Year of Ups and Downs".

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I’ve noticed that the maturity of the Covid cases are found on the East Coast of the US. This doesn’t necessarily mean that it was just because of the big cities found in this area, it’s also caused by the lack of caution and care from the people. Many think that this virus isn’t real until it somehow affects them personally...then it becomes much more real. Let's not wait until we get Covid ourselves, take the precautions. Keep yourself and others safe and out of harm's way. The more we ignore it, the more it’ll grow...and I know for a fact that everyone wants this virus to be done with. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder when we will live life normally again. Go to friends houses and spend the night and travel to amazing new places, meeting new people, going on amazing adventures, all without having to worry about the virus. Scientists predict that the virus will be gone by the end of 2021 but at this rate I’m not so sure that's true. 
What impact does this topic have on you and your community?
We live in a small town and we were doing fairly well with covid and taking precautions and whatnot. We only had a few cases until the college kids came and their school started up again. They had a party, someone with the virus came and it exploded in our community. Cases have sky-rocketed, but only time will tell on how fast things will recover.

We notice the East half of the country has more cases than the West half, and that large population centers and the Southeast have a lot of cases. We noticed the numbers under the state names in the first graph. These seem to be the number of cases in that state. We noticed the first map showed total cases, and the second map showed per capita cases. The darker colors on the first map are overlapping circles, whereas darker colors on the second map represent higher case counts. Places on the first map with really big circles are not always the darkest color on the second map. 

We wonder why the East has more cases. We wonder about the number of deaths per county (or parish, as we call them here in Louisiana). We wonder when this will end, if the rates will go down, and when there will be a vaccine. We wonder what these maps will look like in three months, and what they would have looked like three months ago. 

This data affects our community because not having large social gatherings is making some people lonely and bored. We appreciate that our region’s per capita rate is lower than other parts of the state and the country. The southern part of Louisiana (we are in the northwest corner) is one of the larger red regions on the Per Capita map. We wonder how much Mardi Gras played a role in that.

What's Going On With the East Side?

What do you notice?
	
I notice that there are some discrepancies between the two graphs. For instance, in the total number of cases graph, New York is abundant with cases (it’s bright red!), but in the cases per capita graph, New York is not the most “covidy” state. This tells me that New York has lots of cases, but because of the large population, its cases per capita isn’t that large. Conversely in Louisiana. Its total number of cases isn’t extremely large, but because of its smaller population, its cases per capita is larger. 

Aside from that, I find the circles on the total number of cases graph to be potentially misleading. The larger circles around extremely impacted places (such as New York City) cover areas that aren't necessarily as impacted (such as Hudson, NY). 

What do you wonder?
	I wonder how this graph will change over time and more importantly, which data set tells us more about each state’s Coronavirus count - the total number or cases per capita. 

What impact does this topic have on you and your community?
	These graphs tell me that my city, San Francisco, though not having a massive case per capita, unfortunately has a sizable total number of cases. 

Headline!
	*What’s the State of Coronavirus?*
